evals.prompt: I've been a tier-2 support engineer at Fernwick Logistics for four years. We're a 90-person freight software company and there is nobody here doing developer relations, not even part time, and nobody planning to. I want out of the support queue and into DevRel. I don't code beyond SQL and shell one-liners, and honestly I don't want to learn a real language, it's not where my head is. I've got maybe six hours a week outside work, zero savings buffer, and I'd like to be in a new role within four months. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: A short plan that removes the routes the user's constraints rule out, keeps only the adjacent-role sidestep, and redirects the target from developer advocate to community manager or developer educator, with dated artefact steps and a review point.
expectations: Removes the internal-transfer route from the plan because the employer has no DevRel function, rather than listing it as a lower-priority option
Removes both coding-dependent routes (engineer-to-public-work and learn-to-code-first) rather than ranking them last
Removes community and hackathon volunteering on the grounds that it takes one to two years of unpaid effort the user has no runway for
Identifies the adjacent-role sidestep as the surviving route
States plainly that the realistic targets are community manager or developer educator, rather than leaving the user aimed at developer advocate
Says explicitly that a ruled-out route is deleted from the plan rather than parked at the bottom of a list
Names the four-month deadline, the six-hours-per-week ceiling and the absent savings as the inputs that re-ranked the routes
Does not recommend a coding bootcamp, a computer-science course, or learning a programming language as a prerequisite step
Does not present the entry routes as equally valid options for the user to pick between
Requires the user to pick one technology niche rather than targeting developer relations generally
Recommends publishing a friction log as one of the first artefacts
Names an observable artefact or event for every recommended step rather than describing effort alone
Sets a dated review point with a condition that means changing course rather than pushing harder

evals.prompt: I teach high-school computer science in Leeds, nine years of it. My partner earns enough that I could go without a salary for roughly three years if it came to that, and I have no deadline. What I actually want is the DevRel engineer job at a database company: building the integrations and the sample code, sitting close to product, not the conference-circuit version of the role. I can write Python at teaching level and that's about it. What order should I do things in?
evals.expected_output: A roadmap that promotes the slowest entry route to first because the target role has a code gate, with an intermediate engineering seat, a named niche, and portfolio weighting toward code and developer-voice evidence.
expectations: Promotes the learn-to-code-first route above the default efficiency order rather than leaving it ranked last
Names the product-focused target role as the reason that route is promoted
States that no volume of content or community work substitutes for the recent engineering background these roles screen for
Names the three-year runway and the absence of a deadline as the inputs that promote the slow route
Distinguishes outreach-focused advocate from product-focused advocate and confirms the user is targeting the product-focused variant
Includes an intermediate paid engineering or QA seat as a step on the route rather than going from self-taught code straight to advocate
Says this route reaches a first role in years rather than promising a faster timeline
Notes that an adjacent-role sidestep from teaching would open educator or community-manager roles, not the product-focused role the user wants
Weights code in public and a developer-voice artefact as the heaviest portfolio signals for this target
Requires a single named technology niche rather than databases in general or everything
Does not recommend a developer relations certification or credential as a step
Sets a dated review point with a change-of-course condition

evals.prompt:
Can you look over my DevRel resume? I'm targeting developer advocate roles at observability vendors, the speaking-and-content flavour of the job. Here's the text of it:

'Passionate technologist and community builder. 22,000 followers on X. Wrote many blog posts about Kubernetes and observability. Ghostwrote a guest post for a vendor's engineering blog, published under their CTO's name. Deep-dive piece on OpenTelemetry sampling (Medium, members-only). Gave lightning talks at two local meetups, both recorded. Moderator of a 4,000-member Discord for a tracing project. Grew community engagement 300%. Available for speaking engagements and podcast appearances.'

I mainly want it tuned so it gets past the screening software at the bigger vendors.
evals.expected_output: A six-signal scored audit weighted for an outreach advocate, with explicit deductions named, the applicant-tracking request refused, the missing developer-voice artefact flagged, and at least one line rewritten outcome-first with a link.
expectations: Scores the portfolio against six named signals: public writing, public speaking, code in public, community evidence, teaching artefact, and developer-voice artefact
Uses a 0-3 scale per signal where 0 is absent, 1 is claimed but unevidenced, 2 is evidenced, and 3 is evidenced with an outcome
Weights public writing and public speaking heaviest because the target is an outreach-focused advocate
Scores the unlinked blog-post claim as absent or unevidenced rather than crediting it
Names the 22,000 follower count as a deduction or negative signal rather than a strength
Names the ghostwritten guest post as a negative signal, including that it cannot be defended in a conversational round
Names the members-only or paywalled piece as a negative signal
Names the unsourced 300% figure as an exaggerated or undefendable metric and a deduction
Notes that 'available for speaking engagements' does not count as speaking evidence while a delivered talk does
Credits the two recorded lightning talks as delivered talks
Identifies the missing developer-voice artefact, such as a published friction log, as the biggest single gap
Refuses to optimise the resume for applicant-tracking-system keywords, and says this field hires on public work and referrals instead
Gives a total score and places it in a readiness band rather than only listing fixes
Rewrites at least one resume line so it leads with the outcome and carries a link

evals.prompt: Three years next month as a developer advocate at Karrowin, a 200-person data-pipeline tooling company. I'm the longest-serving person on a team of four. This year I published 14 blog posts, spoke at 6 conferences, our Discord went from 1,200 to 3,900 members, and I ran our booth at two big events. My manager asked me to write up a case for senior before the review cycle closes in five weeks. Help me draft it. My angle is that I've earned it on output alone and I'll pick up the strategy side fast once I'm in the seat.
evals.expected_output: A promotion case rebuilt from activity counts into two or three evidenced behaviour claims mapped to the ladder dimensions, with tenure and potential arguments removed and one honest gap named.
expectations: States that in developer relations promotion recognises work already performed at the next level and is not awarded for potential
Removes or reframes the 'I'll pick up the strategy side once I'm in the seat' argument rather than keeping it in the case
Removes or reframes tenure and longest-serving status as an argument
Names the five ladder dimensions: independence, competence, collaboration, execution, strategic influence
Maps the case to the senior rung defined as improving processes and systems, collaborating org-wide, and factoring company strategy into planning
Says counts of posts, talks and members measure activity rather than the behaviours a level is judged on
Converts at least one of the user's activity counts into an outcome claim tied to a named dimension
Recommends two or three evidenced claims rather than a long list of everything done that year
Requires an artefact or link behind each claim
Recommends naming one honest remaining gap with a plan rather than presenting an unbroken case
Asks whether the employer publishes a written career matrix, and says the absence of one is itself information
Recommends keeping a running evidence log, noting that most developer relations work happens outside a manager's line of sight
Does not build the headline of the case on Discord membership growth

evals.prompt: Found this posting at a Series A company called Quillmark and I'm tempted. 'Developer Advocate I. Requirements: 8+ years professional software engineering across at least four of Go, Rust, Java, TypeScript, Python; demonstrated open-source maintainership; published technical writing portfolio; experience building and moderating developer communities; experience organising conferences and meetups; comfortable with video production and social media management. Salary range $58,000 to $66,000. Reports into Growth Marketing.' Should I tune my CV to hit all those bullets?
evals.expected_output: A read of the posting that names it as a gatekeeper, lists the three symptoms and their root cause, supplies counter-questions for the loop, and gives an explicit apply-or-skip call instead of CV tuning.
expectations: Names this as a gatekeeper posting, using that term
Describes a gatekeeper as a posting that describes an impossible person advertised at entry level and entry pay
Points at the mismatch between the 'Developer Advocate I' title, the $58,000 to $66,000 band, and the eight-plus-years multi-stack requirement
Names the symptom that the posting emphasises skills that are not core to communicating with developers
Names the symptom that the posting is a laundry list of tactics with no statement of the outcomes they serve
Names the symptom that the levelling is inconsistent
States the root cause as a company that does not understand developer relations, and frames it as a working-conditions risk rather than only a hiring-process quirk
Declines to answer by simply tuning the CV to the bullet list
Supplies counter-questions to put to the loop, including what success looks like in twelve months and who measures it
Notes that the Growth Marketing reporting line predicts leads and engagement as the metric
Gives an explicit apply-or-skip call rather than leaving the decision open

evals.prompt: I got approached for 'Founding Developer Advocate' at Nembridge, a 14-person seed-stage API company. The pitch: no DevRel background required, ground-floor ownership, you'd own the docs, the SDKs, the community, developer support, sales engineering calls and customer training, and they'll give me the title Head of Developer Relations. I'd be the only one doing any of it. Compared to my current mid-level advocate job this feels like an enormous step up. What do you think?
evals.expected_output: A read that names the posting as a pit trap, treats the 'head of' title as unlevelled, and lists the founding-role diligence questions to put before any decision.
expectations: Names this as a pit trap, using that term

Describes a pit trap as founding developer relations with ground-floor ownership of docs, SDKs, community, support, sales engineering and training on one person, with no resources, no ladder and no stated goal
Treats 'Head of Developer Relations' as an unlevelled title and tells the user to ask what level it maps to internally
Advises asking for a title that matches the scope before signing rather than after
Names the symptom that the role is a list of tactics with no statement of the outcomes they serve
States the root cause as a company that does not understand developer relations, and frames it as a working-conditions risk
Asks what budget and headcount plan exist
Asks what the company expects developer relations explicitly not to do
Asks who the role reports to
Asks whether a written career matrix exists
Warns about title arbitrage, where the title says advocate but the work is a support queue or a pre-sales calendar, and says to re-score the role as the job it actually is
Does not treat the founding label or the breadth of ownership as evidence of seniority on its own

evals.prompt: Two offers and I have to answer by Friday. Offer A: Senior Developer Advocate at a large cloud provider, $215k base plus stock, I'd sit in an advocacy org of about 30 people, large travel budget. Offer B: Developer Advocate at Sondermere, a seed-stage API startup, $140k plus 1.2% equity on a four-year vest, I'd be their second DevRel hire. B is more exciting but A is obviously the money. Which one do I take?
evals.expected_output: A scorecard that ranks reporting line first, coding-depth expectation second and package last, states the ordering explicitly, and flags that the same title is a different job at each company.
expectations: Scores the offers component by component in the order reporting line, then coding-depth expectation, then package
States that ordering explicitly rather than only implying it through section order
Says the package is the most negotiable component and the least decisive one
Notes that most candidates negotiate hardest over the component that changes their daily job least
States that the reporting line picks the metric: sales buys revenue, marketing buys leads and engagement, engineering buys signups and API use
Instructs the user to ask the reporting line outright in the loop because the posting never states it
Tells the user to confirm the coding-depth expectation against the work rather than the title
Gives the concrete diligence question of asking what the team's last three shipped things were and who wrote them
Notes that large companies level advocates on the software-engineering scale, making the engineering ladder the negotiation anchor there
Does not quote an undated market salary figure as a benchmark for either offer
Warns that 'senior developer advocate' is not portable between a large vendor and a seed-stage startup and means two different jobs
Names the seed-stage expectations concretely, such as generalist breadth across pillars and high coding depth building the demos and the docs
Names publishing rights, travel and conference budget, and the levelling scale used as parts of the package to compare, not only cash and equity
Presents the result as a scorecard or comparison table with a recommendation rather than a prose essay

evals.prompt: Quick one. I'm interviewing for senior developer advocate roles in Berlin, remote-friendly, at Series B-ish infrastructure companies. What number should I be asking for? Just give me a range so I don't anchor myself too low on the call tomorrow.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to quote pay from memory, an explanation that no survey-grade dataset exists, a list of what to check with the evidence grade of each, and a redirect to the package as the real lever.
expectations: Declines to state a salary range from memory
Says an undated pay figure is worse than no figure in a negotiation
States that no survey-grade developer relations compensation dataset exists
Says explicitly whether it can look up current figures, and if it cannot, says so rather than estimating
Names public employer handbooks, salary-sharing threads inside developer relations communities, crowdsourced levelling sites, and devtools recruiters as what to check
Distinguishes a survey with a stated respondent count from crowdsourced levelling data, and notes the latter blends advocates with adjacent engineering roles and reads as a wide directional range
Requires any figure eventually used to carry its source, date, geography and grade
Redirects the user to the package as the real lever: scope, title level, budget, travel policy, publishing rights, equity
Notes that large companies level advocates on the software-engineering scale, making the engineering ladder the anchor there
Records the unresolved pay question as an open question with who to ask, rather than closing it with a guess

evals.prompt: Onsite loop at Voretti, a 120-person dev-tools company, starts a week on Monday. The recruiter just emailed asking me to record a fresh five-minute product demo video 'so the panel can see your style', unpaid, before the first round. I already have four published videos and a conference recording out there. I also have no idea what else is in the loop. Can you help me script the video, and give me some STAR answers to memorise?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to write the unpaid sample with a decline script and a published-work counter-offer, plus format-first prep guidance, a five-story bank in three lengths, and STAR scoped to conversational rounds only.
expectations: Advises declining the unpaid sample video and names it as spec work
States the reasoning that producing a fresh sample when the portfolio is already public is spec work under another name
Offers the published equivalent plus a live working session with the team as the counter-offer
Supplies a short, unapologetic decline script the user can send
Does not write the demo video script as requested
Tells the user to ask the recruiter which formats the loop uses before preparing anything

Lists the developer relations loop formats, including presentation round, content take-home, coding take-home, technical self-rating questionnaire, conversational rounds, DevRel-opinion round, and founder or exec round
Says the DevRel-opinion round is reported as the hardest because it has no right answer to memorise
Restricts STAR to the conversational and behavioural rounds and says it is the wrong shape for the DevRel-opinion round
Tells the user to bank five stories, each prepared in three lengths: roughly two minutes, sixty seconds, and one line

Says to keep only numbers the user can defend under a follow-up question
Tells the user to treat the loop as two-way and evaluate the employer during it, naming pillar mix, funding driver, reporting line and budget
Advises rating honestly on any technical self-rating questionnaire, because inflated self-ratings unravel in the next round

evals.prompt: Presentation round is Thursday and it's Monday night. Forty-five minutes in front of the panel at Grendal Systems. My plan was to write a completely new talk built on their platform and run the whole thing as a live demo against their staging API, which goes down roughly once a day from what I've seen. Sound good?
evals.expected_output: A corrected plan: reuse an existing talk, two timed rehearsals, and a demo engineered with checkpoints, a reset path and a recorded fallback, laid out against the Monday-to-Thursday window.
expectations: Advises reusing and adapting an existing talk rather than writing a new one for the round
Requires at least two full timed rehearsals out loud
Requires a recorded fallback of the demo
Requires independently enterable checkpoints so the demo can be resumed after a failure
Requires a reset path for the demo environment
Names the flaky staging API as the specific risk driving the fallback plan
Gives a day-by-day rehearsal plan anchored to the Monday-to-Thursday window
Includes recording a run and watching it back, fixing only the worst couple of moments
Tells the user to bring one question they genuinely want answered
Tells the user to confirm with the recruiter which other formats the loop contains

evals.prompt: Six years as a senior developer advocate at a large cloud vendor. I've accepted an offer at Tavolino, a 40-person startup whose product is self-serve: individual developers sign up with a card, teams expand later, and sales only gets involved once an account is large. I'm quietly terrified that six years of my experience is worthless there. What actually carries over and what do I have to relearn?
evals.expected_output: A transfer analysis split on go-to-market motion, stating the craft transfers unchanged and the metric definition is the relearning, plus a PLG competency row added alongside the five ladder dimensions.
expectations: States that the craft transfers unchanged, naming writing, speaking, teaching, demo building, friction logging, community facilitation and carrying developer feedback into the company
States that the relearning is which metric the company accepts as proof of impact
Uses go-to-market motion as the comparison axis rather than buyer type or a business-to-business versus business-to-consumer split
Identifies the new company as product-led from the self-serve signup and later team expansion described
Names product-led measurement as activation, expansion revenue, product-qualified-lead volume and product feedback loops
Contrasts that with the large-vendor measurement of attribution and product influence
Warns that 'senior developer advocate' is not portable across company types and means a different job at the startup
Adds a product-led competency gap row covering product-usage evidence, product-qualified-lead scoring, expansion playbooks and developer-to-champion conversion
States that the product-led row sits alongside the five existing dimensions rather than replacing them
Names the shift in the politics-to-output ratio between a big-tech seat and a startup seat
Notes that the reporting line at a product-led company is often engineering or product
Does not frame the move primarily as a pay or equity trade-off

I need to write the job posting for our first developer advocate, work out what the interview loop should be, and figure out how to score the candidates' portfolios when they come in. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A one-line statement that this is the candidate-side skill, a pointer to the employer-side and org-design siblings, and no posting, loop or scorecard produced.

evals.prompt: Two years into an advocate job at Melbrook. I want to be in the top tier of this field within a couple of years and I've written out my plan: build a personal brand, post something every single day on X and LinkedIn, get the follower count up, and stop over-rehearsing my talks. I want that effortless Kelsey Hightower thing where it looks completely off the cuff. Most of my audience lives in our company Slack community, which I run. Sanity-check this for me.
evals.expected_output: A correction of the personal-brand and unrehearsed-style assumptions, the four top-practitioner habits ranked by efficiency with the ranking stated, and the company Slack ruled out as owned distribution.
expectations: States that 'build a personal brand' is mostly wrong advice in this field and that follower count without substance is an explicit negative signal to hiring managers
States that great developer relations centres the developer, not the advocate
Identifies the Kelsey Hightower plan as survivorship-biased
Explains that those talks are built from hundreds of micro-demos rehearsed individually over years, then played like an instrument
Warns that copying 'don't rehearse' without that library fails live
Names the four recurring top-practitioner habits: converting audience signal into internal influence, owning the distribution, treating CFP rejection as iteration, and running consistency as a system
Ranks those four by efficiency, leading with internal influence and then owning the distribution
States the ranking out loud rather than implying it through the order of the list
Says a company Slack or Discord is a walled garden and does not count as owned or public distribution
Notes that only distribution ownership survives leaving the employer, while internal influence stays with the company
Names carrying developer evidence into product decisions as the way to clear the ceiling where developer relations speaks most with customers but holds the least power to act on what it hears
Advises asking for feedback on rejected CFPs and rehearsing at meetups before conferences
Names devrel-company fit as something to weight heavily, and says a strong practitioner in the wrong product, audience or reporting line still underperforms

evals.prompt: Starting from zero here. I'm a QA analyst at Pendrel Health and I want to move into developer relations this year. Two questions. First, which DevRel certification is worth paying for? I keep seeing courses advertising one. Second, I was going to kick things off by submitting to three big conference CFPs next month, since talks seem to be the thing that actually counts. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: A plain statement that no recognised certification exists, plus the ranked first-artefact sequence starting with a friction log, a niche picked from a tool the user already uses, and meetups before conference CFPs.
expectations: States plainly that no recognised developer relations certification exists
Declines to recommend a paid course that implies a credential
Notes that foundation-adjacent technical certifications raise credibility only inside a specific niche such as cloud-native, and only if that is the chosen niche
Ranks the first artefacts by return per day of the user's own work, leading with a friction log
Gives the full order: friction log, blog post, community-answer streak, open-source contribution, meetup talk
States that the meetup talk carries the highest value of the five while losing every efficiency round, and names the condition that promotes it anyway
Recommends a meetup or lightning talk as the rehearsal ground before conference CFPs, rather than opening with three big conference submissions
Requires picking one tool or product the user already uses as the niche before producing artefacts
Notes that a five-minute lightning talk counts toward the published hiring bar of a couple of talks given
States an expectation of roughly six to twelve months of consistent public output before becoming hireable
Names the zero-experience-to-artefacts threshold concretely, such as three substantial posts published and one talk delivered

evals.prompt: I'm a staff-level developer advocate, five years in. My company just offered me 'Head of Developer Relations'. I'd manage one person and inherit the events budget. Same base salary, small title bump. Everybody is congratulating me, but I like building things and I'm not convinced this is actually a promotion. Take it?
evals.expected_output: An unlevelled-title read with the question to ask internally, the two tracks described without ranking one above the other, and the artefact-compounding move named as the IC leverage.
expectations: Treats 'head of' as an unlevelled title and tells the user to ask what level it maps to internally
Advises asking for the title to match the scope, up to director, if the scope is a director's
Refuses to rank the IC track above the management track or the reverse, and says the choice turns on scope preference rather than status
Describes the IC track as raising the strategic share of the work while still executing, with bigger initiatives and cross-org influence at staff and principal
Describes the management track as trading execution for coordination, starting with people management and team goals
Names what a director owns beyond a first-line manager, such as department strategy, metrics, operations, budget, cross-functional relationships and the career ladder itself
Names making each artefact compound as the IC leverage move that reads as senior on either track
Lists concrete downstream uses of one sample app, such as a talk, a conference delivery, a blog post, a video, a social series, a newsletter item, sales enablement and a meetup kit
States that seniority is judged by how far one piece of work travels, not by how many pieces get made
Does not treat managing one person as evidence on its own that the role is a promotion
Names the reporting line and the budget and headcount plan as things to confirm before accepting
